title: Designing Voice Agents for Real Conversations - Chintan Agrawal & Daniel Wirjo, AWS

primary.label: Multimodal & Realtime Systems

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is realtime voice agent systems covering VAD, turn-taking, speech processing, and streaming interaction loops. The workshop addresses voice agent engineering without tying to a specific industry vertical or application domain. Content spans pipeline design, hands-on development with Pipecat, and production concerns like latency budgets and context drift. Prerequisites include familiarity with STT/LLM/TTS pipelines and Pipecat, with live demos involving debug log inspection. Structured as a hands-on workshop with live coding demonstrations and three runnable Pipecat examples. All supporting evidence is directly stated in the transcript with character-anchored excerpts.

summary:
AWS solutions architects Chintan Agrawal and Daniel Wirjo present a workshop on turn-taking in voice agents—how systems know when a user has finished speaking and should respond. They frame this as an audio engineering problem, not an LLM problem: identical models and prompts produce very different experiences depending on the pipeline's responsiveness to interruptions and silence. The core constraint is 200ms, how fast humans switch turns. At 800ms things feel off; at 1.5s users hang up. Salesforce's published best (March 26th) was 755ms, roughly 4x slower than human turn-taking.

The pipeline consists of STT, LLM, and TTS, plus three critical turn-taking components: Voice Activity Detection (VAD) at the front, smart turn detection watching VAD signals and audio features, and an interruption handler that flushes downstream (stops TTS, cancels LLM generation) within about 50ms.

Three levels of turn-taking are presented. Level 1 uses Silero VAD, a 300K-parameter, 2MB model with a single tunable parameter—minimum silence milliseconds—that controls the entire UX but cannot distinguish pause types. Level 2 delegates turn detection to the STT service (Cartesiant ~300ms P50, Deepgram Nova 3 ~250ms P50), adding linguistic context but sacrificing transparency. Level 3 layers Smart Turn V3.2 (8MB, BSD-2 licensed, 58.9% recall, 68.4% precision) on top of local VAD; when the model is not confident, the VAD timer acts as a safety net. Level 3 also enables interruption classification: corrections (stop), fillers (continue quieter), coughs/noise (ignore)—versus today's systems that stop every time.

The latency breakdown (from Daily co-founder Quintela) shows where time goes in a standard cloud API setup: audio capture ~40ms, network/jitter buffer 52ms, STT+endpointing ~300ms, LLM time-to-first-byte 500–650ms (the dominant bottleneck), TTS+playback ~85–120ms—totaling 1,100–1,300ms. Co-locating all models on one GPU cluster achieved ~500ms. STT and LLM together consume about two-thirds of the latency budget, making them the only meaningful levers. LLM benchmarks (June 2026) targeting under 700ms time-to-first-token show Nemotron-3 Ultra at 529ms P50, GPT-4.1 at 536ms P50 but spiking to 1.7s at P95, and Claude 3 exceeding 4s at P95. P95 matters more than P50 for voice because one slow response ruins the entire conversational flow. After 15–20 turns, models begin ignoring parts of the system prompt and become verbose, requiring context pruning or session resets.

Production issues include false interruptions increasing escalation rates, five infrastructure systems that scale and fail independently, and the reality that 755ms remains the best measured cascaded voice-to-voice latency. Daniel then demonstrates all three approaches live with a Pipecat travel assistant using Cartesia STT, Sonic TTS, and Anthropic Claude. The Silero VAD demo shows 300ms threshold cutting off a user mid-thought. The Cartesia STT demo correctly waits for complete sentences. The Smart Turn demo is shown in detail with debug logs: when the user says an incomplete sentence, the end-of-turn state is classified as incomplete but the VAD timer still fires, causing a response—demonstrating the fallback behavior. When the user completes a full sentence, debug logs confirm Smart Turn classifies high probability of sentence completion, triggering an immediate and correct response.

takeaways: Voice agent quality is determined by audio engineering (turn-taking, latency), not the LLM—identical models and prompts produce very different UX depending on pipeline responsiveness.
200ms is the human turn-switching benchmark; at 800ms things feel off, at 1.5s users hang up. Salesforce's best published response time was 755ms, still ~4x slower.
In a standard cloud API setup, total voice-to-voice latency is 1,100–1,300ms; STT and LLM together consume ~2/3 of that budget, making them the only meaningful optimization levers.
LLM P95 tail latency matters more than P50 for voice: GPT-4.1 is 536ms P50 but spikes to 1.7s at P95; Claude 3 exceeds 4s at P95—one slow response ruins the entire flow.
After 15–20 turns, LLMs start ignoring system prompt parts and become verbose, requiring context pruning or session resets.
False interruptions significantly increase human escalation rates—when agents cut people off incorrectly, users request human support.
Smart Turn V3.2 (58.9% recall, 68.4% precision) is the best deployable turn detection today; ~4 of 10 turns fall back to the VAD timer, which can cause premature responses on incomplete utterances.
In practice, teams should combine STT-based turn detection with VAD/silence detection, since each addresses different failure modes.
All three turn-taking approaches share nearly identical Pipecat pipeline code—only the turn-detection analyzer class differs.

sections.title: Introduction & Problem Statement
sections.summary: Chintan and Daniel introduce themselves as AWS APJ startup team solutions architects. They frame turn-taking as an audio engineering problem, not an LLM problem, and show a side-by-side demo where the same user, same model, and same prompt produce very different outcomes—one agent ignores an interruption for ~2s, the other catches it in <200ms and backs off.

sections.title: The 200ms Constraint & Latency Context
sections.summary: 200ms is how fast humans switch turns. At 800ms things feel off; at 1.5s users hang up. Salesforce published 755ms best response time on March 26th, ~4x slower than human turn-taking. The question is how to close this gap or at least get turn-taking right so UX doesn't feel as bad as raw numbers suggest.

sections.title: Pipeline Architecture & Turn-Taking Components
sections.summary: The pipeline has STT, LLM, TTS (audio in, text out, text in, audio out) plus three often-overlooked turn-taking components: VAD (detects speech/silence at the front), smart turn detection (watches VAD signal and audio features to decide whether to respond or wait), and interruption handler (flushes downstream—stops TTS, cancels LLM—within ~50ms on barge-in).

sections.title: Level 1: Silero VAD
sections.summary: Silero VAD is a 300K-parameter, 2MB model using STFT input, four conv layers, LSTM for cross-frame memory, and a sigmoid speech-probability output. Its single tunable parameter—minimum silence ms—controls the entire UX: too low cuts people off mid-thought; too high creates dead air. Domain-dependent (sales ~200ms, thoughtful domains 1000-1200ms). Key limitation: cannot distinguish pause types.

sections.title: Level 2: STT-Based Turn Detection
sections.summary: Cartesiant and Deepgram Nova 3 handle turn detection inside their STT websocket, using full audio signals plus linguistic context. P50 latencies: ~300ms (Cartesiant), ~250ms (Deepgram). Works well when functioning, but trade-off is transparency—when it misfires or cuts someone off, there is no explanation since the decision is made server-side.

sections.title: Level 3: Smart Turn Model
sections.summary: Smart Turn V3.2 runs during silence on top of local VAD: 58.9% recall, 68.4% precision, 8MB, BSD-2 licensed, pip-installable. When not confident (~4 of 10 times), VAD timer fires as safety net at configured latency. Meta's paper reported 87.7% recall but released no code. Level 3 also enables interruption classification: corrections (stop), fillers (continue quieter), coughs/noise (ignore).

sections.title: Interruption Handling & Classification
sections.summary: On barge-in, speech is picked up in ~32ms and pipeline flushed in ~15ms (handled by Pipecat). The key question is whether to stop: red/correction = stop everything, amber/filler = continue quieter, blue/cough-noise = ignore and finish. Most systems today stop every time. The three demo Python files have nearly identical pipelines—only the turn-detection analyzer class differs.

sections.title: Three-Level Summary & Latency Budget Breakdown
sections.summary: Chintan summarizes the three levels: Level 1 (Silero VAD—own silence detection completely), Level 2 (STT provider handles it—smarter but opaque), Level 3 (VAD + Smart Turn—full ownership and portability). He then presents a latency breakdown from Daily co-founder Quintela: audio capture ~40ms, network/jitter 52ms, STT+endpointing ~300ms, LLM time-to-first-byte 500–650ms (dominant bottleneck), TTS+playback ~85–120ms—totaling 1,100–1,300ms. Co-located GPU clusters achieved ~500ms. STT and LLM together consume ~2/3 of the latency budget, making them the only meaningful optimization levers.

sections.title: LLM Benchmarks & Multi-Turn Challenges
sections.summary: Benchmarks (June 2026) targeting under 700ms time-to-first-token show Nemotron-3 Ultra at 529ms P50, GPT-4.1 at 536ms P50 but 1.7s P95, and Claude 3 exceeding 4s at P95. P95 matters more than P50 for voice—one slow response ruins the entire flow. After 15–20 turns, models start ignoring system prompt parts, become verbose, and go off-spirit, requiring context pruning or session resets.

sections.title: Production Issues & Infrastructure
sections.summary: Production issues include false interruptions increasing human escalation rates, five systems that scale and fail independently, and 755ms still being the best measured cascaded voice-to-voice latency. Smart Turn's 58.9% recall is the best deployable today, with ~4 of 10 turns falling back to VAD timer. Options include Picovoice Cloud for managed hosting or AWS guidance reference architecture for enterprise deployments.

sections.title: Daniel's Hands-On Demo: Three Turn-Detection Examples
sections.summary: Daniel demonstrates three Pipecat examples with a travel assistant (Cartesia STT, Sonic TTS, Anthropic Claude). Silero VAD demo: 300ms stop parameter causes premature turn end when user pauses mid-sentence. Cartesia STT demo: correctly detects incomplete vs. complete sentences, waits for full sentence before responding. Smart Turn demo: debug logs show end-of-turn state classified as incomplete when user says 'I'm thinking of going to um,' but VAD timer still fires causing a response—demonstrating the fallback behavior. When user completes a full sentence ('I'm actually thinking of um going to Sydney'), debug logs confirm Smart Turn classifies high probability of sentence completion, triggering correct immediate response. Daniel notes in practice you'd combine both STT-based turn detection and VAD/silence detection, as each addresses different failure modes including barge-in interruption handling.
